title: The Magnificent Golden Gate Bridge
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in transcript as iHeart Intro for Chuck) record on the Golden Gate Bridge, covering the origin of the name 'Golden Gate' (John Frémont, 1846), early ferry service and the push for a bridge (Charles Crocker, 1872), the 1916 and 1921 proposals and Joseph Strauss's hybrid design, Charles Ellis's math work and firing, the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District and its 1923 vote and 1930 bond financing with Bank of America's A.P. Giannini, construction from 1933 (hard hats, safety net, 11 deaths), International Orange paint, opening in 1937, wind-driven stiffening decisions, seismic retrofit, and the bridge's suicide history, the 2006 documentary The Bridge, and the safety net installed in 2024. Ends with listener mail and friends-of-the-show plugs.
topics: Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District

entities.name: Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode recorded on the Golden Gate Bridge, discuss an upcoming comedy show appearance, and talk about favorite bridges.

segments.title: Introduction to the Golden Gate Bridge
segments.summary: The bridge is described as often named the most photographed bridge in the world and one of the seven Wonders of the modern World, and was named a Bridge of the Millennium by ASCE in 2000. The name predates the bridge.

segments.title: Origin of the name Golden Gate
segments.summary: In 1846 army officer John Frémont named the strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific, first in Greek as chrysopylae and later in English as the Golden Gate.

segments.title: Geography and early ferry travel
segments.summary: The strait is about 300 feet deep, the bay much shallower. San Francisco is a peninsula, so reaching the north required crossing the strait. Ferries were expensive and the first official ferry, the Princess, ran in 1868. Charles Crocker proposed a bridge in 1872 for railroad reasons.

segments.title: Early bridge proposals and Strauss's hybrid design
segments.summary: In 1916 journalist James Wilkins proposed a 3,000-foot suspension bridge at a cost of about 100 million dollars, which was dismissed. City engineer Michael O'Shaughnessy later sought a cheaper option and engineer Joseph Strauss proposed a combined suspension and cantilever design at about 17 million dollars.

segments.title: Strauss and Charles Ellis
segments.summary: Strauss is described as the central figure and is often credited with building the bridge, though many contributed. Charles Ellis, a math-focused engineer who had worked on Hudson River tunnel plans, was hired to handle the structural math.

segments.title: Financing, the 1923 district act, and opposition
segments.summary: The 1923 Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District Act let surrounding counties vote on a tax district that could borrow money; about six of 21 counties joined. Opponents included rural counties, the Sierra Club, earthquake concerns after 1906, shipping interests, the Department of War, and the Southern Pacific Railroad, which ran ferries. Lawsuits followed, and supporters prevailed.
topics: Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District

segments.title: Early design criticism and redesign
segments.summary: The first hybrid design was criticized as looking like an upside-down rat trap. Ellis, with consulting engineers including Leon Moisseiff and Ollie Amman, and Strauss, moved to a full suspension design, tall and long.

segments.title: Hand calculations, scale model testing, and Ellis's firing
segments.summary: Engineers did calculations by hand without computers, and tested a 1:156 scale model at Princeton. Strauss grew irritated with Ellis's math and fired him by telegram after forcing a vacation. Ellis received little credit until after his death in 1949, and he re-checked the figures unpaid during the Depression.

segments.title: Bond sales and Bank of America
segments.summary: In November 1930 the district issued 35 million dollars in bonds, but buyers were scarce during the Depression. A.P. Giannini, president of Bank of America, bought about six million dollars' worth.

segments.title: Construction start and site challenges
segments.summary: Construction began January 5, 1933 amid fog, storms, high winds, and strong tides. The north tower sat on sturdy rock on the Marin side, while the south tower was about 1,000 feet offshore on serpentine rock. Geologist Andrew C. Lawson tested the bedrock, and he was described as going down in a diving bell.

segments.title: Foundations, fenders and bumper-bowling tangent
segments.summary: Workers blasted rock underwater, a trestle road was built to the offshore tower, and oval concrete fenders protect the towers from ships. The hosts digress into bowling.

segments.title: Steel, towers, and International Orange
segments.summary: Bethlehem Steel supplied about 44,000 tons of steel per tower, shipped by barge through the Panama Canal. Temporary elevators were added later. Consulting architect Irving Morrow helped choose the orange color, a primer-based hue that became Golden Gate International Orange; silver, black, and black-and-yellow were rejected.

segments.title: Aesthetics and the color debate
segments.summary: Morrow designed tower panels that decrease in size from bottom to top to look taller. The hosts discuss the color choice and International Orange used in life vests.

segments.title: Safety record and deaths during construction
segments.summary: Strauss required hard hats and used a movable safety net that saved 19 workers, known as the Halfway to Hell Club. In February 1937 scaffolding collapsed; the net failed and ten died, bringing the total construction deaths to eleven.

segments.title: Main cables and completion
segments.summary: The four cables each contain about 25,000 wires and were spun by John A. Roebling's Sons. The bridge was completed April 19, 1937, about a million under the 35 million dollar budget. Pedestrians crossed first, then cars.

segments.title: Strauss's poem and credit
segments.summary: At the opening Strauss read a poem he wrote, 'The Mighty Task Is Done', which the hosts criticize for not mentioning Ellis. Strauss has a bronze statue in Golden Gate Park.

segments.title: Design choices: no rail tracks and wind stiffening
segments.summary: Wind concerns after the Tacoma Narrows collapse led to horizontal trusses that added weight, which ruled out railroad tracks. The bridge held the longest suspension span record until 1964, when the Verrazzano-Narrows took over.

segments.title: Earthquake survival and maintenance
segments.summary: The bridge survived the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake with little damage while a section of the Bay Bridge collapsed. The bridge is in constant painting and corrosion maintenance. A later seismic retrofit addressed an eight-point-six San Andreas quake, including bolting towers to foundations.

segments.title: Suicides at the bridge, prevention, and the safety net
segments.summary: The bridge has long been a site of suicides, averaging about twenty a year, and volunteers and others stopped many. Harold Weber was the first recorded suicide in 1937. The official count stopped at 997 in 1995; credible estimates exceed 2,000. The 2006 documentary The Bridge was controversial. A safety net finished in early 2024 cost 224 million dollars and reduced suicides by 73 percent. A 1970s study followed up on people stopped from jumping. Hosts invite listeners who volunteer on the bridge to write in.

segments.title: Pop culture: James Bond
segments.summary: Hosts note the Golden Gate Bridge appears in the James Bond film The Man Who Never Dies... specifically, the hosts say Bond defeats Christopher Walken on the bridge in A View to a Kill.

segments.title: Listener mail and friends of the show
segments.summary: The hosts plug the McElroy brothers' The Adventure Zone, a tabletop role-playing podcast, and discuss movies and podcast appearances. A listener, Ryan Pinto, is mentioned about the Denver show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts promote live show tickets in Denver, Seattle, and San Francisco and give the email address, then sign off.
